facts.fact: Stray voltage happens when faulty equipment leaks current into the tank water.
There is usually no warning of stray voltage until the current finds a path to ground, and a person can become that path.
An ordinary outlet does not cut the power when a person gets a shock.
Warning signs of a failing pump include weaker flow, unusual noise, vibration, too much heat, running on and off, trouble starting and higher power use.
Pump noise is often caused by vibration, trapped air or a dirty impeller.
Noise often comes from debris in the impeller chamber, a worn shaft or bearing, or the pump vibrating against the glass or cabinet.
Strong vibration usually comes from worn bushings, a damaged shaft or a badly placed pump.
Weak flow is usually caused by blockages or debris inside the pump, or by kinks or airlocks in the tubing.
Weak flow can also come from a dirty impeller, a blocked intake, clogged filter media or trapped air.
A pump that will not start often has a seized impeller or calcium (limescale) buildup.
A pump that runs on and off may be overheating or may have loose connections, worn motor parts or debris inside.
Running a pump dry can overheat it and damage it for good.
Some pumps have dry-run protection: the SuperFish PondECO Plus E stops after 10 seconds without water flow and tries again every 10 seconds. After 5 tries it stops for good.
If the SuperFish PondECO Plus E motor overheats, the pump switches itself off and starts again after about 15–20 minutes of cooling.
If a plug or socket gets wet, do not pull the plug out. Switch off the fuse or circuit breaker that feeds it.
Do not use a pump whose cord or plug is damaged, or one that has been dropped, damaged or is not working properly.
After a dry-run shutdown of the SuperFish PondECO Plus E, make sure water reaches the pump, unplug it, wait 60 seconds and plug it back in.
After the SuperFish PondECO Plus E shuts down from overheating, find and fix the cause of the overheating.
Unplug the pump before you take it out of the tank to clean it.
Unplug the pump whenever it is not in use, and before adding or removing parts or cleaning it.
To clean: unplug the pump, take it out, take it apart as the maker describes, and check for dirt, algae, broken impeller blades, worn shafts and damaged bushings.
Clean the impeller, shaft and housing with a soft brush, and rinse the parts in tank water rather than tap water.
Check the shaft for wear, bending or damage while the pump is apart.
When putting the pump back together, check that every part sits correctly before switching it on.
After reassembly the impeller should turn freely, moving about halfway before it springs back into place.
If the noise continues after cleaning, check for loose fittings and airlocks in the tubing.
Clean inlet grills, tubing and filter sponges to bring back weak flow.
Do not try to repair a pump yourself. Take it to an authorised service centre or throw it away.
Think about replacing a pump if it needs frequent repairs, if flow stays poor after cleaning, if electrical problems develop, if spare parts are unavailable or if the noise becomes excessive.
A seized or limescale-blocked pump may start again after a thorough clean, but a damaged rotor needs a replacement part.
Use the pump only on a circuit protected by a ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI).
Protect aquarium circuits with GFCI outlets or GFCI/AFCI breakers. A breaker in the main panel is often easier to fit when outlets are hidden behind the stand.
Make a drip loop in every cord that runs from the pump to an outlet, so water drips off the cord instead of reaching the socket.
Mount power strips firmly, away from water and splashes, and do not plug one power strip into another.
Dry your hands before plugging or unplugging equipment, and wear dry rubber-soled shoes when working on the tank.
Never let the pump run dry: it must be fully under water while it runs.
Unplug pumps and heaters before the water level drops so far that they run dry.
Keep the pump fully under water, on a flat surface, and not touching the tank walls or decorations.
Clean the pump every 4–6 weeks to stop blockages building up.
Check pumps every 2–3 months in lightly stocked freshwater tanks and monthly in heavily stocked tanks.

Maintenance plan: every month check flow, listen for noise and look at the intake strainers. Every 2–3 months clean the impeller chamber. Every 6–12 months replace worn impellers and check seals, O-rings and power cables.
Choose the right pump size: one too small struggles to move the water, and one too large makes strong flow that stresses fish.
Plug the SuperFish PondECO Plus E only into an earthed socket kept dry, and check that the voltage on its label matches your supply.
The SuperFish PondECO Plus E manual says the water it pumps must never be hotter than 35°C.
Do not use soap or chemicals on pump parts. Rinse them in tank water, not tap water, to protect beneficial bacteria.
Do not handle a pump with wet hands.
Ground probes are hotly debated. Reef Builders says that if you use one, plug it into a GFCI-protected outlet, because it gives stray voltage a path to ground.

Vietnamese shop blogs use these terms: CB (circuit breaker), chống giật (ELCB/RCCB residual-current breaker), cánh quạt (impeller), mô tơ/cuộn dây (motor/windings), ổn áp (voltage stabiliser), cột áp (head pressure).
Pump brands sold in Vietnam include Atman, Baoyu, Hsbao, Jebao, Jingye, Periha, Sobo and SunSun.
During power cuts, the heater and pump/filter can be run from another power source such as a generator.
The longer fish stay in unfiltered water during a power cut, the worse the water gets. If ammonia rises above 1 ppm, change 10 to 30 percent of the water.
Do not feed fish while the pump is off in an outage, because digestion uses oxygen in warm months. Stirring the water with a whisk raises dissolved oxygen.
